objective: Make every workflow install its Python dependencies from the hash-checked lock, so the environment a CI or release check runs in is the same one the image was built from.
decision_supported: Does the repository actually install from the hashed lock everywhere it claims to, and can a test prove it rather than searching for substrings?
acceptance: No workflow installs a package from a version range.
Every workflow that needs project dependencies installs them with --require-hashes -r docker/requirements-dev.lock followed by --no-deps -e .
pip itself may still be upgraded, because it cannot be hash-locked from the same file.
The test walks each install command instead of asserting that three strings appear somewhere in a file.
The test fails when a bare install is added to any workflow.
evidence: Before the change, five workflows resolved dependencies from ranges: ci.yml installed 'pyyaml pytest' and four others installed '.[dev]'.
The previous test only asserted that three files contained three strings, so a range install alongside them passed.
Injecting 'python3 -m pip install pyyaml' into daily-smoke.yml makes the new test fail with the offending command named; reverting it passes.
stop_conditions: A workflow turns out to need a package the lock does not carry; that package belongs in pyproject and the lock, not in a bare install.
The editable project cannot be installed with --no-deps because a runtime dependency is missing from the lock.
risks_and_fallbacks: The lock now governs more workflows, so a stale lock breaks more jobs at once; that is the point, and the verifier already fails loudly.
pip upgrade stays unhashed because it bootstraps the hashing itself; the test allows exactly that one command and nothing else.
